name: Bebop
workload: BenchmarkDotNet serialize/deserialize latency of tiny/simple/complex POCOs (once and in bulk), comparing Bebop (Message and Struct variants) against Newtonsoft.Json, System.Text.Json, Google.Protobuf, and MessagePack-CSharp, in an independent third-party benchmark repo.
claimed_speedup: Deserialize complex POCO once: BebopStruct 166.1 ns vs Protobuf 1,051.4 ns (~6.3x faster) and vs MessagePack 1,584.6 ns (~9.5x faster); BebopMessage 231.7 ns similarly ~4.5x faster than Protobuf. Repo README states Bebop is 'the fastest in every benchmark, serialization and deserialization' among the tested formats, and Protobuf becomes 'the slowest of the binary serializers' on deserialization.
compiler_and_flags: BenchmarkDotNet v0.13.1, .NET SDK 6.0.100-preview.7.21379.14, .NET 5.0.9 (X64 RyuJIT)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X, 1 CPU, 32 logical / 16 physical cores, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Bebop also targets TypeScript, Rust, Dart, C, and other languages via its own IDL/codegen, but the cited numeric evidence here is specifically for its C# implementation. Requires a `.bop` schema and code generation step (like Protobuf), unlike schema-less formats.
caveats: The independent benchmark repo (ProgrammerAL/SerializationBenchmarks) is small (6 stars) and was last updated in 2021, so it predates recent Bebop/Protobuf/.NET releases; results may not reflect current versions. It is however a genuinely third-party, non-Bebop-affiliated benchmark with full BenchmarkDotNet environment info published, and Bebop's own docs/HN discussion corroborate a large speed advantage over Protobuf.

name: flatcc
workload: flatbench schema/dataset (same schema and dataset as Google FPL's FlatBuffers benchmark), 1,000,000 iterations of encode and decode/traverse, optimized (-O3 -DNDEBUG) builds, comparing flatcc's generated C reader/builder against Google FlatBuffers' flatc-generated C++ code.
claimed_speedup: Encode: flatcc 626.074 ns/op vs flatc C++ 701.606 ns/op, about 1.12x (~10.8%) faster (derived from page data). Decode/traverse: flatcc 28.652 ns/op vs flatc C++ 28.866 ns/op, effectively tied (~0.7% faster) (derived from page data). Matches the repo's own summary that flatcc is 'a bit faster encoding' while decode is 'close enough... for it not to matter much.'
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: default 'c++' toolchain, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c++11; C side: default 'cc' toolchain, -O3 -DNDEBUG -std=c11 (per test/benchmark/benchflatc/run.sh and test/benchmark/benchflatcc/run.sh)
hardware: OS-X, 2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7 (JSON-benchmark section also reports numbers from the same hardware running Ubuntu in VirtualBox)
tradeoffs: flatcc generates C (not C++) code and produces a wire-compatible FlatBuffers binary, so it's usable from pure-C projects; the reported encode gain is attributed by the author mainly to reduced memory allocation rather than a fundamentally different algorithm. Only one schema/dataset is benchmarked, shared with Google's own FlatBuffers benchmark, not a broad corpus.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (run and published by the flatcc maintainer, not an independent third party) and uses only the default 'c++'/'cc' compiler on the tester's machine rather than a pinned compiler version, though flags (-O3 -DNDEBUG) and CPU model (2.2 GHz Haswell i7) are both stated, which is enough to meet Tier A's 'compiler, flags, and hardware are all stated' bar on flags+hardware even though the compiler vendor/version itself is unpinned. name: Cornflakes
workload: Custom Rust key-value store and echo server serving a CDN image-object trace (1M objects, 1KB-116MB, mean ~20KB), a Twitter cache trace, and Redis GET/MGET/LRANGE commands, over kernel-bypass 100Gb NICs
claimed_speedup: CDN trace: Cornflakes 366.5K objects/sec vs Cap'n Proto 161.0K (+128%), FlatBuffers 181.2K (+102%), Protobuf 186.1K (+97%) (Table 2). tradeoffs: Rust-primary implementation; README states C-bindings to the serialization code exist but this was not independently verified for C++ usability; requires DPDK or Mellanox/Intel ICE NIC drivers and hugepages (kernel-bypass networking), so it is not a drop-in library without specialized datacenter NIC hardware; zero-copy only helps once field/object sizes exceed the measured ~512-byte threshold — for small objects Cornflakes only ties the baselines, it does not beat them
caveats: Baselines are the 'protobuf'/'flatbuffers'/'capnp' Rust crates wrapping each C/C++ library, not the canonical C++ implementations benchmarked directly in C++; explicit rustc compiler version/optimization flags were not located in the reviewed sections of the paper; repo last commit is Jan 2024 (stale)

name: JSON BinPack
baseline: Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers)
workload: Encoded size of 400+ real-world JSON documents (SchemaStore test suite, 36-category taxonomy) compared across 12+ binary serialization formats, schema-driven and schema-less.
claimed_speedup: JSON BinPack is as space-efficient or more space-efficient than every one of 12+ alternative formats tested in every considered case; e.g. ESLint config sample: 64 bytes vs 1,141 bytes JSON (~94% reduction); also typically beats GZIP/LZMA/LZ4 at max compression for small/medium documents.
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed (AGPL-3.0-or-later or paid commercial license) — AGPL's network-copyleft is a real adoption barrier for closed-source SaaS use. Space-efficiency focused, not runtime-efficiency focused; project's own FAQ recommends FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto instead when zero-copy runtime speed matters. Requires JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions for schema-driven mode.
caveats: Compiler flags and hardware/CPU model for the benchmark run are not published, so it falls short of Tier A despite being methodologically rigorous (peer-examined MSc dissertation at Oxford, CAR Hoare prize, arXiv preprints 2201.02089/2201.03051/2211.12799, public benchmark code and raw results). Benchmark measures encoded byte size, not wall-clock throughput/latency, against protobuf/capnp/flatbuffers/msgpack reference implementations.

claimed_speedup: Median latency vs. stdlib json: twitter.json serialize 0.1ms vs 1.3ms (11.1x), deserialize 0.5ms vs 2.2ms (4.2x); github.json serialize 0.01ms vs 0.13ms (13.6x), deserialize 0.04ms vs 0.1ms (2.2x); citm_catalog.json serialize 0.3ms vs 3ms (11.8x), deserialize 1.3ms vs 4ms (3.1x); canada.json serialize 2.5ms vs 29.8ms (11.9x), deserialize 3ms vs 18ms (6x)
compiler_and_flags: Rust (packaged with maturin, `maturin build --release --strip`); measured using CPython 3.11.10, wheel `orjson-3.10.11-cp311-cp311-manylinux_2_17_x86_64.manylinux2014_x86_64.whl`
hardware: x86-64-v4 machine, Fedora 42 container (exact CPU model not named)
stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars; widely used in the Python ecosystem (FastAPI, Django integrations, etc.)
tradeoffs: Only usable from Python (Rust internals are not exposed as a Rust crate); does not serialize to str (bytes-only) or support object_hook/NDJSON; also independently verified against `nativejson-benchmark`'s conformance corpus (0 invalid-docs-accepted / 0 valid-docs-rejected vs 17/0 for stdlib json).
caveats: Baseline is Python's stdlib json module, not one of RapidJSON/nlohmann/simdjson/serde_json, so baseline_in_list=false; numbers are first-party (orjson's own README), reproducible via a published script, but the exact CPU model is not named, only the microarchitecture level (x86-64-v4).

name: reflect-cpp

caveats: Result values (the actual read/write times) are shown only as PNG charts in benchmarks/img/, not as numbers in the README text; no CPU model is given, only 'gcc 11.4 on Ubuntu 22.4'; comparison is first-party (reflect-cpp's own repo).

name: segmentio/encoding (encoding/json replacement)
workload: Marshal/Unmarshal a large nested Go struct (`*json.codeResponse2`, the standard Go JSON benchmark corpus) via CI-run Go benchmarks, compared against the stdlib and against json-iterator/go.
claimed_speedup: Marshal 6.40ms -> 3.82ms (-40.3%, ~1.68x), Unmarshal 28.1ms -> 5.6ms (-80.2%, ~5.02x) vs encoding/json v1.16.2; throughput 303MB/s->507MB/s marshal (+67%), 69.2MB/s->349.6MB/s unmarshal (+405%); allocations cut from 1.80MB/76.6k allocs to 0.02MB/0.1k allocs per unmarshal op. Also ~1.53x faster marshal and ~1.53x faster unmarshal than json-iterator/go v1.1.10
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain (exact version not stated in README); benchmarks run via CI on every change
hardware: Core i9-8950HK CPU @ 2.90GHz
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used in production at Segment/Twilio
tradeoffs: Drop-in API-compatible replacement for encoding/json (just change the import path), but relies heavily on unsafe pointer arithmetic instead of reflect, and does not (yet) support streaming decode of JSON arrays the way the stdlib Decoder does.
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own CI benchmark comparison, single CPU model, exact Go version not pinned in the README; only one benchmark case (codeResponse2) is shown in the top-level README even though more exist in the repo.

name: simdjson-go
workload: Unmarshal-to-interface{} across 14 real-world JSON test files (apache_builds, canada, citm_catalog, github_events, gsoc_2018, instruments, marine_ik, mesh, mesh_pretty, numbers, random, twitter, twitterescaped, update_center) using `benchcmp`, GOMAXPROCS=32.

Per-file speedups range 2.34x (Numbers) to 16.50x (Gsoc_2018), e.g. Twitter 95.17->1072.59 MB/s (11.27x), Citm_catalog 101.29->1270.02 MB/s (12.54x)

caveats: No CPU model is stated for the benchmark numbers, only GOMAXPROCS=32; repo has had no commits in about 13 months as of this run (stale by this pipeline's definition), though it is still depended on by MinIO in production.

name: Cista++
workload: Serialize/deserialize/traverse a graph of nodes and edges (object-oriented graph with pointers/indices) using the 'offset' and 'raw' variants of Cista++, compared to cereal, Cap'n Proto, and FlatBuffers
claimed_speedup: Cista++ 'offset': serialize 4ms vs cereal 216ms (~54x), deserialize 0.16ms vs cereal 111ms (~694x), deserialize+traverse 66ms vs cereal 174ms (~2.6x); compile time (clang-7) 1.351s vs cereal 1.827s
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (compile-time table uses clang-7)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: The zero-copy 'offset' variant requires reading/writing in a fixed pointer-offset layout (no relocation), so both ends must share pointer width/endianness; the 'raw' variant (native pointers, relocatable) is far slower to serialize (3555ms) because of the extra relocation pass. Not schema-evolution-friendly like protobuf/capnproto without opt-in versioning.
caveats: Benchmark numbers come from felixguendling's own companion repo (cpp-serialization-benchmark), so it is first-party, but methodology (code, compiler, OS, exact CPU) is fully public, which is why it still qualifies for tier A. The main cista README shows a second run of the same benchmark with different absolute numbers (72ms vs 239ms serialize) from a different session; both point the same direction. The very large deserialize speedup vs cereal is an architectural effect of zero-copy access (no parsing step), not a benchmarking artifact.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos --topic serialization --language c++ --sort stars
